# Implement block: Spirograph Draw (SwiftUI)

You are adding the "Spirograph Draw" block from Native Cook to the user's iOS app. The block already exists as working SwiftUI code. Your job is to bring it into this project faithfully, not to write a new one that looks similar.

## The block

A spirograph on a pad of cream drawing paper lying on a dark desk: a clear plastic ring with 96 inward teeth, printed ticks and its size, and inside it a tinted translucent gear with five pen holes and a pen standing in one of them. Dragging round the ring rolls the gear and the pen draws a hypotrochoid in real ink that builds up into a rosette, while the rest of the closed pattern shows faintly in pencil; until anything is drawn a small arrow sweeps round the ring to show the way. A header reads "Spirograph" with the gear, hole and loop count ("40-tooth gear · hole 3 · 12 loops") and a Clear button; under the pad a hint and three rows of controls pick the gear (30, 40, 56 or 72 teeth), the pen hole (1–5) and the ink (ultramarine, vermilion, viridian or graphite). Inks overlap like real ink, a tap on the paper moves the pen to the next hole, and Clear tears the top sheet off the pad.

**Motion.** The paper is a square under the header, as wide as the screen less 16 pt a side (smaller if the height needs it), with the ring scaled to sit 12 pt inside it. A gear of n teeth has a pitch radius of 150·n/96 model units; its centre runs round a circle of 150 − r at the angle φ, and it turns by −(150 − r)/r for every radian of φ, so a 40-tooth gear closes its pattern after 5 turns (12 loops) and a 72-tooth one after 3 (4 loops). A drag that starts on the paper rolls the gear by the finger's change of angle around the ring's centre (ignored within 18 pt of it); a release keeps it rolling at the finger's angular speed (at most 14 rad/s), slowed by friction of 1.1 /s until it falls under 0.04 rad/s, and any touch stops it. The pen samples the curve every 0.016 rad of rolling into 1.35-unit round-capped strokes; strokes are cut into chunks of 96 points, each recorded once, and every 24 chunks are flattened into one offscreen image, so the drawing is only ever appended to and its cost stays bounded. The ink layer is multiplied onto the paper. The pencil preview of the whole closed pattern morphs with the gear and hole and fades out at 4 /s once the pen has covered the whole pattern (a success haptic when that happens by hand). A hole change moves the pen on a critically damped spring (stiffness 170, damping 26); a gear change crossfades the old gear out, shrinking 8%, as the new one grows in over 0.45 s; a new ink starts a new stroke; the pen lifts during the changes. Clear slides the top sheet off to the left and down by its width plus 90 pt, turning 9° about its top edge, over 1.05 s (cubic ease-in-out) with a lifted shadow, uncovering a fresh sheet. The coach arrow shows while the sheet is empty and nothing moves (fading at 5 /s): every 2 s it sweeps 1.2 rad round the ring just ahead of the gear (cubic ease-out over 1.1 s), holds and fades over the last 0.4 s. Haptics: a selection tick for a hole or an ink, a light impact for a gear, a medium one for Clear. The self-playing demo starts on a clean sheet with the 40-tooth gear, hole 3 and ultramarine, rolls it 5 times round from 0.9 s over 5.6 s, switches to vermilion at 7 s and the 72-tooth gear at 7.4 s, moves the pen to hole 5 at 7.9 s, rolls 3 times round from 8.4 s over 3.6 s, tears the sheet off at 12.7 s, sets the 40-tooth gear, hole 3 and ultramarine back at 14.2 s and repeats every 16 s; a touch pauses it for 4 s. One fixed 1/60 s tick drives the rolling, the pen, the script and every transition, at most 3 ticks a frame. Under reduced motion the demo does not play, a release does not coast, hole and gear changes are instant and Clear fades the sheet out in 0.35 s.

## Reference source

The block is built and running in the Native Cook source repository. Each link below is a file on GitHub. To read one as plain text, replace `https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/` with `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/` in its address.

### Demo (start here)

- [SpirographDrawDemo.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Playground/SpirographDraw/SpirographDrawDemo.swift)

### Files of the block

- [SpirographDraw.metal](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Playground/SpirographDraw/SpirographDraw.metal)
- [SpirographDraw.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Playground/SpirographDraw/SpirographDraw.swift)
- [SpirographDrawEngine.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Playground/SpirographDraw/SpirographDrawEngine.swift)
- [SpirographDrawModel.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Playground/SpirographDraw/SpirographDrawModel.swift)

### Shared helpers the block uses

- [swift/NativeCook/Shared/ComponentSupport.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Shared/ComponentSupport.swift)

### Frameworks

It needs no framework beyond SwiftUI.

## Your instructions

_Anything specific to this app goes here: where the block should appear, what to rename, what to change. Left empty, integrate the block as it is._

## How to work

Work like an experienced iOS engineer joining an existing project: learn the app first, read only what you need, decide early how the block fits, then integrate it with as little disruption as possible. Take the steps in order.

**Done means** the block is reachable in the user's app and behaves like the reference in the iOS Simulator or on a device. A SwiftUI preview is useful while you work, but it is not the proof: build and run the app.

**Fidelity.** Bring over the real implementation. Keep its structure, colours, sizes, timings and curves. Change only what this project requires and what "Your instructions" ask for.

If you already learned this project earlier in the conversation, reuse what you know and skip step 2. Learn it again only if the project changed or something you need is missing.

### 1. Check where you are

- You need the project's files and a terminal. If this prompt was pasted into a chat that has neither, stop and say so: it has to be run by a coding agent opened on the project.
- Confirm the project is an iOS app built with Xcode (an `.xcodeproj`, an `.xcworkspace` or a Swift package with an app target). If it is something else, stop, say what you found, and do not create a new app inside it unless the instructions ask for one.

### 2. Learn the host app

- The app target, its deployment target and its Swift version.
- SwiftUI, UIKit or both, and how a screen is shown today: `NavigationStack`, a coordinator, a tab bar, a storyboard.
- How files join the target: a folder the project synchronises, or a file list in the project that you have to extend.
- Conventions: folder layout, naming, where colours, fonts and assets live.
- Type names the app already uses, so the block's types do not collide with them.

### 3. Read the block

- Swift files in a module do not import each other, so the demo alone will not lead you to the rest. The list above names every file of the block: read them all.
- The demo is how the source repository shows the block. Bring over what the demo shows, not the repository's gallery. Anything listed under "Used by the demo only" stays behind.
- Read the block's initialiser and its defaults. The demo may switch on an option that makes the block play by itself for a recording (for example `autoPlay`). Keep the option; leave it off in the user's app unless asked.

### 4. Decide the fit

- The source app targets iOS 17. If the host targets an older system, check each API the block uses and tell the user what would have to change before you lower anything. Do not raise the host's deployment target without asking.
- If a type or function name of the block already exists in the app, rename the block's one, in every file that uses it, and say that you did.
- Shared helpers: copy the ones the block uses next to it, or fold them into the block's files. Do not copy helpers it never calls.
- In a UIKit app, show the block through a `UIHostingController`.

### 5. Bring it in

- Add the block's files to the app target, keeping their names.
- Copy its asset catalogs, loose resources and fonts, and check that the names the code asks for match the names in the bundle: a wrong name compiles and then shows nothing.
- A `.metal` file has to be compiled into the same target as the code that calls its function.
- Keep reduced-motion handling, haptics and accessibility labels as they are in the source.
- Mount the block where the instructions say. With no instructions, add a screen named after the block and make it reachable the way the app's other screens are.

### 6. Run it

- Build the app target for a simulator with `xcodebuild` or the project's own script, and fix every error and new warning the block introduced.
- Run it and use the block: every state, every gesture, light and dark appearance if the block follows them, and once with Reduce Motion on.
- If the build or the simulator fails for a reason outside the block, report the error and ask how to continue.

### 7. Report

- Files added and changed, and anything renamed to avoid a collision.
- How to reach the block in the app.
- Anything that differs from the reference, and why.
